title: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In such cases the geometrical ratio of increase, the result of which never fails to be surprising, simply explains the extraordinarily rapid increase and wide diffusion of naturalised productions in their new homes.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Rapid increase of naturalised animals and plants”. Scope: introduced and feral animals and plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Spread data are extensive, but paired fertility and mortality data are available only for selected invasions. Thus exponential spread is testable broadly while the asserted exclusive demographic explanation is only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For dated introductions, fit spread and abundance trajectories using intrinsic growth, fertility in native versus introduced ranges, and stage-specific mortality. Rapid spread explained by reduced mortality without increased fertility supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A specific dataset URL may not encode abundance or demography.

Enemy release, adaptation and propagule pressure are confounded.

Introduction dates and early absences are uncertain.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.64
data existence: 0.84
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.61
operationalizability: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Naturalization inventories and range products document rapid spread, and demographic matrices contain the fecundity-versus-survival contrast for a subset. The mechanism is testable where both ranges have vital rates and is only inferred from occurrence elsewhere. Animal invasions and evolved fertility changes keep the full statement partly unresolved.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare fecundity of species in native versus introduced ranges, and compare survival or population growth over the same contrast, for naturalized plants and animals. Rapid spread with unchanged fecundity and higher survival would support geometrical increase under lower mortality; a systematic rise in fertility sufficient to explain the increase would count against the stated mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
GloNAF covers plants, while the statement also includes animals.

Evolved increases in fecundity and enemy-release effects on body size can raise fertility after introduction.

Vital-rate comparisons in both ranges exist for far fewer species than naturalization records.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.44
analysis feasibility: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.52
data existence: 0.62
operationalizability: 0.7
